section_1.title: The Intuition: Same Reality, Different Maps
section_1.content: Introduce the concept of a coordinate system as a 'language' to describe a vector. Establish the prerequisite: A basis is a set of linearly independent vectors that span the space. Use a visual of a squirrel (the vector) needing to be located on a grid. Different observers (bases) use different 'units' to describe the same squirrel.
section_1.example: A squirrel sits at point (3, 2) in a standard grid. If a bird sees the world through a stretched, tilted grid, it perceives the same squirrel at different coordinates.

section_2.title: Defining the Transformation Matrix
section_2.content: Explain how to bridge two bases (B and C). Represent the basis vectors of B as coordinates within basis C. These columns form the Change-of-Basis Matrix (P). Use an animation where basis vectors slide and rotate to align with the new coordinate system.
section_2.example: If basis B = {b1, b2} and basis C = {c1, c2}, the matrix P is [ [b1]c | [b2]c ]. Applying P converts a vector 'v' from B-coordinates to C-coordinates: [v]c = P[v]b.

section_3.title: Step-by-Step Computational Workflow
section_3.content: Provide a clear, algorithmic approach: 1. Express the 'old' basis vectors in terms of the 'new' basis. 2. Arrange these as columns to form the transition matrix P. 3. Multiply the original coordinate vector by P.
section_3.example: Translating a robot's arm position from 'Global World Coordinates' to 'Arm-Segment Local Coordinates' using a 2x2 transition matrix.

section_4.title: Synthesis and Visualization
section_4.content: Consolidate the concept: Changing basis is a 'perspective shift,' not a change in the vector's actual position in space. The vector is the physical object; the coordinates are just the numerical representation based on our chosen 'ruler'.
section_4.example: A video game character (the vector) remains in the same spot, but changing the camera view (the basis) changes how the game engine calculates the character's position on the screen.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                # Adjusted for 6x6 grid on the right half
                x = 2.0 + j * 0.8  # Starting further right
                y = 2.0 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
